y-m-43-01.title: Checking Hyeonu's expansion solution
y-m-43-01.topic: Matrix multiplication and the commutative law: expanding (A+B)^2
y-m-43-01.goal: Check line by line whether an expansion rule that you naturally use in calculations with numbers is also used for matrices as it is, make matrices where the rule breaks, and judge the features of matrices for which the rule survives.
y-m-43-01.material: A matrix is written row by row, and what is before the semicolon (;) is the first row. For example, [1 1 ; 0 1] is the matrix whose first row is 1, 1 and second row is 0, 1. E is the identity matrix [1 0 ; 0 1], and O is the zero matrix with all entries 0. There are two matrices A=[1 1 ; 0 1] and B=[1 0 ; 1 1]. Hyeonu expanded (A+B)^2 as below. Suppose only the agreements for adding and multiplying matrices may be used on each line, and find the line written without grounds. (In the expressions, A^2 is the matrix A multiplied twice.)
y-m-43-01.thinking.0: Find the line that skipped ahead without grounds in the solution
y-m-43-01.thinking.1: Make examples where the rule does not hold (counterexamples) yourself
y-m-43-01.thinking.2: Sort out the condition for the cases where the rule holds
y-m-43-01.prereq.0: This task's H3 is only a marker of the difficulty and support level of this production assignment, not a sign that the curriculum assigns it to that grade. It assumes you have already learned the definition of a matrix and the sum, product, and identity matrix of 2×2 matrices.
y-m-43-01.prereq.1: Calculating the product of 2×2 matrices (pairing the entries of the first row and the first column and adding, and so on)
y-m-43-01.prereq.2: The expansion of numbers (a+b)^2=a^2+2ab+b^2 (middle school grade 3 level)
y-m-43-01.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in Hyeonu's solution that cannot come out from the agreements alone. Some lines also look correct in calculation.
y-m-43-01.s.s1.hint.0: Compare each line with the line right before it and find what changed.
y-m-43-01.s.s1.hint.1: With A and B of this problem, calculate AB and BA directly and compare whether the two results are the same.
y-m-43-01.s.s1.line.1: = A·A + A·B + B·A + B·B   (distribute, but keep the order of multiplying as it is)
y-m-43-01.s.s1.line.2: = A^2 + AB + AB + B^2   (assume writing AB instead of BA is the same)
y-m-43-01.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is the problem. Line 2 has AB and BA separately, but line 3 rewrote BA as AB. For numbers ab=ba, so swapping is allowed, but for matrices there is no agreement that AB and BA are equal. Line 4 is a result that carried over that rewriting, so it is an expression that does not hold in general. But this does not mean this solution is wrong for any A, B. In cases where AB and BA are equal, it holds as it is. Check in the following steps.
y-m-43-01.s.s2.prompt: Keep A=[1 1 ; 0 1] as it is, and make two different B=[p q ; r s] for which AB and BA are different. The entries p, q, r, s are integers from -3 to 3.
y-m-43-01.s.s2.hint.0: Let the entries of B be p, q, r, s and write the four entries of AB and BA each.
y-m-43-01.s.s2.hint.1: Put the entries of AB and BA side by side one by one and find which entries can differ.
y-m-43-01.s.s2.var.p: Entry p in the first row, first column of B
y-m-43-01.s.s2.var.q: Entry q in the first row, second column of B
y-m-43-01.s.s2.var.r: Entry r in the second row, first column of B
y-m-43-01.s.s2.var.s: Entry s in the second row, second column of B
y-m-43-01.s.s2.ok.c1: The entries are integers from -3 to 3.
y-m-43-01.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make the entries integers from -3 to 3.
y-m-43-01.s.s2.ok.c2: AB and BA are different. Hyeonu's last expression breaks for this B.
y-m-43-01.s.s2.fail.c2: AB and BA are the same. Calculate the four entries of the two products one by one and compare.
y-m-43-01.s.s2.explain: For example, if B=[1 0 ; 1 1], then AB=[2 1 ; 1 1] and BA=[1 1 ; 1 2], which differ. Since (A+B)^2 - (A^2+2AB+B^2) = BA - AB, for B where AB and BA differ, Hyeonu's last expression is wrong. For this A, if the entry in the second row, first column of B is not 0, or the two diagonal entries of B are different, then AB and BA become different.
y-m-43-01.s.s3.prompt: Choose all the B for which (A+B)^2 = A^2 + 2AB + B^2 actually holds when A=[1 1 ; 0 1]. Do not choose by eye; it is fine to check some of them by calculating directly.
y-m-43-01.s.s3.hint.0: Put the expanded form of (A+B)^2 side by side with A^2+2AB+B^2, and organize how their difference is written with AB and BA.
y-m-43-01.s.s3.hint.1: Before calculating AB and BA for each candidate, first check the entries that separated AB and BA in the previous step (the entry in the second row, first column, and the difference of the two diagonal entries).
y-m-43-01.s.s3.r.a: This is exactly the B for which AB and BA were different in the previous step. You may not yet have connected that the condition for the expression to hold is 'AB and BA are equal'.
y-m-43-01.s.s3.r.c: It has an upper triangular shape like A, so it may look the same, but if you judge only by the feeling that the shapes are similar, you miss the difference between AB and BA. Calculate directly.
y-m-43-01.s.s3.explain: (A+B)^2 = A^2 + 2AB + B^2 holds exactly when AB=BA. For this A to have AB=BA, the entry in the second row, first column of B must be 0 and the two diagonal entries must be equal. [2 0 ; 0 2], [3 5 ; 0 3], [0 1 ; 0 0] are such cases, and [1 0 ; 1 1] and [1 2 ; 0 2] are not. Even if most of the entries are 0, you must check separately whether AB=BA.

y-m-43-02.title: Checking Yerin's 'like numbers' reasoning
y-m-43-02.topic: Two matrices whose product is the zero matrix (AB=O)
y-m-43-02.goal: Test whether a property that holds for numbers may be carried over to matrices as it is, make an example where AB=O but neither A nor B is the zero matrix and explain why using a property of A, and choose the conditions under which the conclusion holds.
y-m-43-02.material: A matrix is written row by row, and what is before the semicolon (;) is the first row. For example, [1 1 ; 0 1] is the matrix whose first row is 1, 1 and second row is 0, 1. E is the identity matrix [1 0 ; 0 1], and O is the zero matrix with all entries 0. For numbers, if ab=0 then a=0 or b=0. Yerin said, 'Matrices also have rules for adding and multiplying, so if AB=O then A=O or B=O.' In this task A=[1 2 ; 2 4] is fixed, and A is not the zero matrix.
y-m-43-02.thinking.0: Find the line where a conclusion was drawn by analogy ('like numbers')
y-m-43-02.thinking.1: Make an example where it does not hold and explain why
y-m-43-02.thinking.2: Judge the conditions under which the conclusion holds
y-m-43-02.prereq.0: This task's H3 is only a marker of the difficulty and support level of this production assignment, not a sign that the curriculum assigns it to that grade. It assumes you have already learned the definition of a matrix and the sum, product, and identity matrix of 2×2 matrices.
y-m-43-02.prereq.2: The fact that for numbers, if ab=0 then a=0 or b=0 (middle school level)
y-m-43-02.prereq.3: The earlier experience that having an inverse matrix means there is a matrix that gives E when multiplied
y-m-43-02.s.s1.prompt: Choose one line in Yerin's story that lacks grounds.
y-m-43-02.s.s1.hint.0: Sort each line into a statement about numbers, a statement about matrices, or a conclusion.
y-m-43-02.s.s1.hint.1: Find the line that could be the grounds for line 3, and compare whether it says something in the same direction as line 3.
y-m-43-02.s.s1.line.0: For numbers, if ab=0 then a=0 or b=0.
y-m-43-02.s.s1.line.1: Matrices also have rules for adding and multiplying, like numbers.
y-m-43-02.s.s1.line.2: Therefore for matrices too, if AB=O then A=O or B=O.
y-m-43-02.s.s1.line.3: In fact, if A=O then AB=O whatever B is.
y-m-43-02.s.s1.explain: Line 3 is a leap. Line 1 is a correct fact about numbers, and line 2 only says that matrices also have rules, not that they are 'the same rules as numbers'. Line 4 is also correct, but it says only one direction, 'if A=O then AB=O'. What line 3 needs is the opposite direction (if AB=O then A=O or B=O), so line 4 does not support line 3. Whether a property that holds for numbers also holds for matrices must be tested separately.
y-m-43-02.s.s2.prompt: For A=[1 2 ; 2 4], make two different B=[p q ; r s] with AB=O where B is not the zero matrix. Then explain below why such a B exists.
y-m-43-02.s.s2.hint.0: Write the four entries of AB in terms of p, q, r, s, set each to 0, and count how many different equations come out.
y-m-43-02.s.s2.hint.1: Look separately at the equations for the first column (p, r) and for the second column (q, s), and choose values that satisfy them one by one.
y-m-43-02.s.s2.var.p: Entry p in the first row, first column of B
y-m-43-02.s.s2.var.q: Entry q in the first row, second column of B
y-m-43-02.s.s2.var.r: Entry r in the second row, first column of B
y-m-43-02.s.s2.var.s: Entry s in the second row, second column of B
y-m-43-02.s.s2.ok.c1: The first row of AB is all 0.
y-m-43-02.s.s2.fail.c1: The first row of AB has a non-zero entry. Write the first-row entries in terms of p, q, r, s.
y-m-43-02.s.s2.ok.c2: The second row of AB is also all 0. So AB=O.
y-m-43-02.s.s2.fail.c2: The second row of AB has a non-zero entry.
y-m-43-02.s.s2.ok.c3: B is not the zero matrix.
y-m-43-02.s.s2.fail.c3: B is the zero matrix. You need to find a B that is not the zero matrix.
y-m-43-02.s.s2.explain: For example, if B=[-2 0 ; 1 0], then AB=[0 0 ; 0 0]. Neither A nor B is the zero matrix but the product is the zero matrix, so line 3 of Yerin does not hold. Giving one example is enough to break 'always'. This time, B that are constant multiples of each other (for example [-2 0 ; 1 0] and [-4 0 ; 2 0]) are also counted as different examples.
y-m-43-02.s.s2.because.prompt: For the B you just made, write in one or two sentences why AB becomes the zero matrix, citing one property of A.
y-m-43-02.s.s2.because.hint.0: With the B you made above, write the value you get by multiplying the first row of A with the first column of B and adding.
y-m-43-02.s.s2.because.hint.1: Put the two rows of A (1, 2 and 2, 4) side by side and first write in one sentence what relation they have.
y-m-43-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.0: Does the reason you wrote reach a property of A (that its determinant is 0, that its rows are proportional, and so on), or did you just repeat 'because AB is O'?
y-m-43-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.1: Did you actually multiply one B you made by A and check with numbers that it becomes the zero matrix?
y-m-43-02.s.s2.because.selfAssess.2: Did you think about whether the same B would still work if A changed (for example A=[1 0 ; 0 1])?
y-m-43-02.s.s2.because.model.0: The determinant of A is 1×4-2×2=0, so there is no inverse matrix. So if you take one column of B like (-2, 1), the product with A gives 0, and AB=O can happen even when B is not the zero matrix.
y-m-43-02.s.s2.because.model.1: The second row of A is 2 times the first row, so if you make only one row 0, the second row becomes 0 automatically. If you take the column of B as (2, -1), then 1×2+2×(-1)=0.
y-m-43-02.s.s2.because.modelNote.1: Another model answer, explained by the proportional relation of the rows.
y-m-43-02.s.s3.prompt: When A is not the zero matrix, what condition lets you conclude 'if AB=O then B=O'?
y-m-43-02.s.s3.hint.0: Recall this A and the B you made in the previous step, and check one by one whether each condition holds for that A.
y-m-43-02.s.s3.hint.1: First explain in words why, for numbers, ab=0 and a≠0 lets you say b=0, using 'divide by a', and then think about what plays the role of dividing in matrices.
y-m-43-02.s.s3.o.a: All the entries of A are non-zero numbers
y-m-43-02.s.s3.r.a: This A=[1 2 ; 2 4] also has all entries non-zero, but there was an example where B is not the zero matrix. Connecting with the example from the previous step, this condition is not enough.
y-m-43-02.s.s3.o.b: A^2, the square of A, is also not the zero matrix
y-m-43-02.s.s3.r.b: A^2=[5 10 ; 10 20] is also not the zero matrix, but there was an example with B≠O. The situation is the same when you take powers of A.
y-m-43-02.s.s3.o.c: There is a matrix that gives E when multiplied with A
y-m-43-02.s.s3.o.d: A is a square matrix (2×2) and is not the zero matrix
y-m-43-02.s.s3.r.d: This A was also 2×2 and a counterexample appeared. The size of the matrix does not guarantee this conclusion.
y-m-43-02.s.s3.explain: If A has an inverse matrix A^(-1), multiplying A^(-1) on the left of both sides of AB=O gives B=O. This is the same as the condition that the determinant is not 0. Conversely, if the determinant is 0, an example with B≠O can arise, as it did this time.

y-m-43-03.title: Putting a point that was moved twice back to the start
y-m-43-03.topic: The order of successive transformations and inverse matrices
y-m-43-03.goal: Judge what you need to know to undo the result of doing two transformations in a row, choose the matrix that undoes it, and find directly points for which the result is the same when the order is changed.
y-m-43-03.material: A matrix is written row by row, and what is before the semicolon (;) is the first row. For example, [1 1 ; 0 1] is the matrix whose first row is 1, 1 and second row is 0, 1. E is the identity matrix [1 0 ; 0 1], and O is the zero matrix with all entries 0. A point (x, y) is written as the column vector [x ; y], and a matrix is multiplied from the left to move the point. The matrix A=[1 1 ; 0 1] moves the point (x, y) to (x+y, y), and B=[2 0 ; 0 1] moves the point (x, y) to (2x, y). A and B both have inverse matrices. A and B were applied once each, in some order, one after the other, to some point. We know only the resulting point and want to recover the original point. The inverse matrix of A is written A^(-1), and the inverse matrix of B is written B^(-1).
y-m-43-03.thinking.0: Judge what more information is needed
y-m-43-03.thinking.1: Work out how the order of successive transformations affects the result
y-m-43-03.thinking.2: Find directly the cases that do not depend on the order
y-m-43-03.prereq.0: This task's H3 is only a marker of the difficulty and support level of this production assignment, not a sign that the curriculum assigns it to that grade. It assumes you have already learned the definition of a matrix and the sum, product, and identity matrix of 2×2 matrices.
y-m-43-03.prereq.1: Products of 2×2 matrices and the calculation of multiplying a column vector by a matrix
y-m-43-03.prereq.2: Being able to accept the meaning of an inverse matrix (a matrix that gives E when multiplied) and the fact that when two matrices both have inverse matrices, their product also has an inverse matrix
y-m-43-03.s.s1.prompt: Chaerin said, 'We did the transformation twice and A and B each have an inverse matrix, so we can recover the original point.' To decide how to recover it, what else must we know besides this?
y-m-43-03.s.s1.hint.0: For the point (1, 2), follow the resulting point in the case where A is done first and then B, and in the case where B is done first and then A.
y-m-43-03.s.s1.hint.1: Compare whether the resulting points of the two cases are the same, and if they are not, think about whether the way to undo them could be the same.
y-m-43-03.s.s1.o.a: The x-coordinate and y-coordinate of the original point
y-m-43-03.s.s1.r.a: If you know the original point, you do not need to recover it. How to undo is decided not by the values of the point but by the order of the transformations and the matrices.
y-m-43-03.s.s1.o.b: Which of A and B was applied first
y-m-43-03.s.s1.o.c: Whether A^(-1) and B^(-1) are the same matrix
y-m-43-03.s.s1.r.c: A and B are different, so the two inverse matrices are also different. Whether they are the same is not information that decides how to undo.
y-m-43-03.s.s1.o.d: Whether the resulting point is not the origin
y-m-43-03.s.s1.r.d: Whether the result is the origin or not, you undo it with the same matrix. You may have thought the method depends on the values of the point.
y-m-43-03.s.s1.explain: How to undo depends on 'what was done first'. If you apply A first and then B to the point (1, 2), it becomes (6, 2), and if you apply B first and then A, it becomes (4, 2). The results are different, so the way to undo cannot be the same. The values of the point are not needed to decide the matrix that undoes.
y-m-43-03.s.s2.prompt: Now you know that 'A was done first and then B'. What matrix gives back the original point when multiplied onto the resulting point?
y-m-43-03.s.s2.hint.0: The original point (1, 2) became (6, 2) by A then B. Apply each candidate to this (6, 2) and check whether (1, 2) comes back.
y-m-43-03.s.s2.hint.1: When a product of matrices is applied to a point, decide whether the right matrix or the left matrix is applied first, and match it with which matrix was the last transformation.
y-m-43-03.s.s2.r.a: When you multiply the matrix product B^(-1)A^(-1) onto a point, the right one, A^(-1), is applied first. Compare this with the order in which you undo starting from the last transformation.
y-m-43-03.s.s2.r.b: The matrix that adds the two undoings does not undo the point twice but adds the two results. Applying in succession and adding are different.
y-m-43-03.s.s2.r.c: The inverse matrix of A+B is not the inverse of applying A and B in succession. A sum is a different operation from doing one after another.
y-m-43-03.s.s2.explain: If the point is moved by A and then B, the resulting point is B(A x) (the original point x multiplied first by A and then that result multiplied by B). To undo it, you must first undo the last one done, B (B^(-1)), and then undo A (A^(-1)). When multiplying matrices, the right matrix is applied first, so it is A^(-1)B^(-1). Example: when the original point (1, 2) became (6, 2), B^(-1) gives (3, 2) and A^(-1) brings back (1, 2).
y-m-43-03.s.s3.prompt: Is there a point for which the result is the same whatever the order? Find and enter two different integer points (x, y), not the origin, for which 'the result of doing A first and then B' and 'the result of doing B first and then A' are the same.
y-m-43-03.s.s3.hint.0: Write in terms of x and y the coordinates of the point obtained by applying A first and then B to the point (x, y). Write the case where B is done first in the same way.
y-m-43-03.s.s3.hint.1: When you set the first coordinates of the two points equal, look at what relation between x and y remains.
y-m-43-03.s.s3.ok.c1: It is a point with integer coordinates and x is not 0.
y-m-43-03.s.s3.fail.c1: Please make it a point with integer coordinates and x not 0.
y-m-43-03.s.s3.ok.c2: The results of the two orders are the same. (The first coordinate is the same, and the second coordinate is always y.)
y-m-43-03.s.s3.fail.c2: The results of the two orders are different. Write the result of A first then B and the result of B first then A each as (x, y) and compare.
y-m-43-03.s.s3.explain: If you do A first and then B, (x, y) goes through (x+y, y) and becomes (2x+2y, y). If you do B first and then A, it goes through (2x, y) and becomes (2x+y, y). For the first coordinates to be equal, 2y=y, that is, y=0. So the order does not matter only for points on the x-axis, and for other points the order changes the result.

y-m-43-04.title: Being calculable and having meaning
y-m-43-04.topic: The meaning of a matrix product: the rows and columns of a quantity table and a price table
y-m-43-04.goal: Tell apart what can be calculated when two tables are multiplied and what makes the result meaningful, interpret the meaning of the entries of the result, and explain what one entry of the calculation with the order swapped counts.
y-m-43-04.material: A matrix is written row by row, and what is before the semicolon (;) is the first row. For example, [1 1 ; 0 1] is the matrix whose first row is 1, 1 and second row is 0, 1. E is the identity matrix [1 0 ; 0 1], and O is the zero matrix with all entries 0. At a school, Class 1 and Class 2 buy bread and milk as snacks. The quantity table N has rows for classes (first row Class 1, second row Class 2) and columns for items (first column bread, second column milk): N=[3 2 ; 1 4]. (Class 1 buys 3 breads and 2 milks, Class 2 buys 1 bread and 4 milks.) The price table P has rows for items (first row bread, second row milk) and columns for shops (first column shop X, second column shop Y): P=[1500 1800 ; 1000 1200]. (The unit is 원. At shop X, bread is 1500원 and milk is 1000원 / at shop Y, bread is 1800원 and milk is 1200원.) They want to find out the total cost for each class and each shop. Jiho said, 'Just multiply N and P in this order,' and Seoa said, 'Both are 2×2, so multiplying P and N also can be calculated, so the order does not matter.'
y-m-43-04.thinking.0: Judge by telling apart calculability and meaning
y-m-43-04.thinking.1: Interpret the entries of the product in the words of the situation
y-m-43-04.thinking.2: Write the conclusion supported by concrete numbers
y-m-43-04.prereq.0: This task's H3 is only a marker of the difficulty and support level of this production assignment, not a sign that the curriculum assigns it to that grade. It assumes you have already learned the definition of a matrix and the sum, product, and identity matrix of 2×2 matrices.
y-m-43-04.prereq.2: The experience of writing a table as a matrix (rows are horizontal lines, columns are vertical lines)
y-m-43-04.s.s1.prompt: Choose the most suitable judgment about Seoa's statement.
y-m-43-04.s.s1.hint.0: Write one line each on what the rows and what the columns refer to in N and P.
y-m-43-04.s.s1.hint.1: When calculating one entry of a product, write which line of the front matrix and which line of the back matrix are paired, and compare whether the paired lines refer to the same thing.
y-m-43-04.s.s1.o.a: Correct. Both matrices are 2×2 so the product is defined, and in either order a total with the same meaning comes out
y-m-43-04.s.s1.r.a: You may have taken being able to calculate the product as meaning the result is meaningful. Work out whether being calculated and having meaning are the same.
y-m-43-04.s.s1.o.b: It cannot be judged. You have to calculate in both orders and compare the sizes
y-m-43-04.s.s1.r.b: Calculating directly is a good method, but the meaning of the result comes not from the size of the numbers but from what the rows and columns of the multiplied tables refer to.
y-m-43-04.s.s1.o.c: Wrong. Multiplying P and N can be calculated but does not have the meaning of totals by class and shop
y-m-43-04.s.s1.o.d: Correct. In either order the result is a value in 원, so it can be read as an amount of money
y-m-43-04.s.s1.r.d: You may have judged only because the units are the same. Check whether you can say which class spent the money at which shop for each entry.
y-m-43-04.s.s1.explain: An entry of a product is the value from pairing one row of the front matrix and one column of the back matrix, multiplying, and adding. So what the columns of the front matrix refer to (the columns of N are items) and what the rows of the back matrix refer to (the rows of P are items) must be the same for it to make sense. PN can be calculated, but it pairs and multiplies the columns of P (shops) with the rows of N (classes), so it has no meaning.
y-m-43-04.s.s2.prompt: In the matrix NP, the product of N and P in Jiho's order, what does the entry in the second row, first column (5500) represent?
y-m-43-04.s.s2.hint.0: Write out as a product expression which row of N and which column of P the 5500 was calculated from.
y-m-43-04.s.s2.hint.1: Turn each product in the expression you wrote out into words as 'the count of what' and 'the price of what'.
y-m-43-04.s.s2.o.a: The total cost (원) when Class 2 buys at shop X
y-m-43-04.s.s2.o.b: The value of Class 2's number of breads times shop X's price of bread
y-m-43-04.s.s2.r.b: This is only one part of the sum (bread only). Check the two products that make up the entry to see whether you left out the milk share.
y-m-43-04.s.s2.o.c: The price difference between shop X and shop Y
y-m-43-04.s.s2.r.c: Looking at the components of the products that make up the entry, the prices of shop Y are not in it. Check the line being multiplied.
y-m-43-04.s.s2.o.d: The sum of the amounts Class 1 and Class 2 spent at shop X
y-m-43-04.s.s2.r.d: Class 1's quantities are not in this entry. Check that the row refers to a class.
y-m-43-04.s.s2.explain: The entry in the second row, first column of NP pairs the second row of N (Class 2: bread 1, milk 4) with the first column of P (shop X: bread 1500, milk 1000) and is 1×1500+4×1000=5500. It is the total cost when Class 2 buys at shop X.
y-m-43-04.s.s3.prompt: Seoa wants to read the entry 6300 (=1500×3+1800×1) in the first row, first column of PN, the product of P and N, as 'Class 1's amount'. Point out which numbers this 6300 comes from multiplying and adding, and judge and write whether it can be read as a meaningful value.

y-m-43-05.title: Collecting matrices that become the identity matrix when squared
y-m-43-05.topic: Matrices satisfying A^2=E and their common properties
y-m-43-05.goal: Confirm by making examples that the solutions of x^2=1 for numbers, only two, are far more numerous for matrices, find and sort out common properties among the examples you made, and explain with calculation why this differs from numbers.
y-m-43-05.material: A matrix is written row by row, and what is before the semicolon (;) is the first row. For example, [1 1 ; 0 1] is the matrix whose first row is 1, 1 and second row is 0, 1. E is the identity matrix [1 0 ; 0 1], and O is the zero matrix with all entries 0. For a number x, if x^2=1 then x=1 or x=-1. For a 2×2 matrix A=[a b ; c d], find A that satisfies A^2=E. The entries need not be integers, but if you approximate a square-root value by a decimal, a correct answer may come out as incorrect, so it is better to use integers or numbers that come out exactly, like 0.6 and 0.8. (A^2 is the matrix A multiplied twice, not each entry squared.)
y-m-43-05.thinking.0: Make directly several examples that satisfy the constraints
y-m-43-05.thinking.1: Find common properties among the examples and sort out generalizations
y-m-43-05.thinking.2: Explain the point where properties of numbers and properties of matrices part ways
y-m-43-05.prereq.0: This task's H3 is only a marker of the difficulty and support level of this production assignment, not a sign that the curriculum assigns it to that grade. It assumes you have already learned the definition of a matrix and the sum, product, and identity matrix of 2×2 matrices.
y-m-43-05.prereq.1: Calculating the square of a 2×2 matrix
y-m-43-05.prereq.2: The fact that the solutions of x^2=1 for numbers are 1 and -1
y-m-43-05.prereq.3: If integer calculations are hard, you may use fractions or decimals that come out exactly
y-m-43-05.s.s1.prompt: Make three different matrices A=[a b ; c d] with A^2=E where A is neither E nor -E.
y-m-43-05.s.s1.hint.0: Write the four entries of A^2 in terms of a, b, c, d and write the equations that set each equal to the corresponding entry of E.
y-m-43-05.s.s1.hint.1: Think by splitting into the case b=c=0 and the case where b or c is not 0.
y-m-43-05.s.s1.var.a: Entry a in the first row, first column
y-m-43-05.s.s1.var.b: Entry b in the first row, second column
y-m-43-05.s.s1.var.c: Entry c in the second row, first column
y-m-43-05.s.s1.var.d: Entry d in the second row, second column
y-m-43-05.s.s1.ok.c1: The first row, first column entry of A^2 is 1.
y-m-43-05.s.s1.fail.c1: The first row, first column entry of A^2 (a×a+b×c) is not 1.
y-m-43-05.s.s1.ok.c2: The first row, second column entry of A^2 is 0.
y-m-43-05.s.s1.fail.c2: The first row, second column entry of A^2 (a×b+b×d) is not 0.
y-m-43-05.s.s1.ok.c3: The second row, first column entry of A^2 is 0.
y-m-43-05.s.s1.fail.c3: The second row, first column entry of A^2 (c×a+d×c) is not 0.
y-m-43-05.s.s1.ok.c4: The second row, second column entry of A^2 is 1. So A^2=E.
y-m-43-05.s.s1.fail.c4: The second row, second column entry of A^2 (c×b+d×d) is not 1.
y-m-43-05.s.s1.fail.c5: A is E. You need to find a matrix that is not E.
y-m-43-05.s.s1.fail.c6: A is -E. You need to find a matrix that is not -E.
y-m-43-05.s.s1.explain: For example, [1 0 ; 0 -1], [0 1 ; 1 0], [1 2 ; 0 -1], [3 2 ; -4 -3], [0.6 0.8 ; 0.8 -0.6] all satisfy A^2=E. For numbers, x^2=1 has only two solutions, but for matrices there are infinitely many like this.
y-m-43-05.s.s2.prompt: Think while recalling examples different from the ones you just made. Choose all the things that must hold for every matrix A=[a b ; c d] with A^2=E where A is neither E nor -E.
y-m-43-05.s.s2.hint.0: For the examples you made, find a+d and ad-bc each and organize them in a table.
y-m-43-05.s.s2.hint.1: For each option, find an example that breaks it among the examples you made, or make a new one. If it does not break, think about the reason once more before regarding it as holding.
y-m-43-05.s.s2.o.a: a, b, c, d are all non-zero
y-m-43-05.s.s2.r.a: There are examples with 0 mixed in, like [1 0 ; 0 -1]. Check whether any of the examples you made breaks this statement.
y-m-43-05.s.s2.o.b: a+d=0 (the sum of the diagonal entries is 0)
y-m-43-05.s.s2.r.c: For [1 2 ; 0 -1], b=2 and c=0. You may have generalized after looking only at symmetric examples ([0 1 ; 1 0]).
y-m-43-05.s.s2.r.e: [0.6 0.8 ; 0.8 -0.6] also satisfies A^2=E. This may be a generalization that arose because you only made integer examples.
y-m-43-05.s.s2.explain: If A^2=E and A is neither E nor -E, then a+d=0 and ad-bc=-1. The reason is that A^2=E gives b(a+d)=0 and c(a+d)=0; if b=c=0, then a and d are ±1 and (a, d)=(1, -1) or (-1, 1) is needed for A to be neither E nor -E, so a+d=0, and if b or c is not 0, then a+d=0. Then from a^2+bc=1, ad-bc=-a^2-bc=-1. The entries need not be integers, need not all be non-zero, and b=c is not required.
y-m-43-05.s.s3.prompt: For a number x, the solutions of x^2=1 are only 1 and -1, but for matrices there are many more. Pick one A you made above, calculate the entries of A^2 directly to show it, and write in one or two sentences why this differs from numbers.
y-m-43-05.s.s3.hint.0: Write the four entries of the A you chose one by one according to the rule of products.
y-m-43-05.s.s3.hint.1: In the calculation of each entry, look at what value each of the two added terms is, and what happens in the entries where the sum is 0.
y-m-43-05.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you calculate the square of the A you chose entry by entry and show that E comes out?
y-m-43-05.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did the 'reason it differs from numbers' come from the product rule that entries get mixed and added, or did you just repeat 'because it is a matrix'?
y-m-43-05.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about why the reason that x^2=1 for numbers has only two solutions (factoring and so on) is not used the same way for matrices?
y-m-43-05.s.s3.model.0: If A=[0 1 ; 1 0], the first entry of A^2 is 0×0+1×1=1 and the other entries are 0×1+1×0=0. Terms that become 0 arise in the sums of products, and it becomes E. This is because, unlike the square of a number, several entries are mixed and added.
y-m-43-05.s.s3.model.1: In [3 2 ; -4 -3]^2, the (1, 1) entry is 3×3+2×(-4)=1 and the (1, 2) entry is 3×2+2×(-3)=0. Positive and negative terms cancel each other and it becomes E, and in x^2 of a number there is no such cancelling.
y-m-43-05.s.s3.modelNote.1: A model answer that gives cancelling as the reason.
y-m-43-05.prereq.4: Calculating ad-bc (the difference of the diagonal products) for a 2×2 matrix [a b ; c d]. This value is used in s2 and is usually called the determinant.
y-m-43-05.s.s3.model.2: If A=[0 1 ; 1 0], then A^2=E and (A-E)(A+E)=A^2-E=O. But neither A-E=[-1 1 ; 1 -1] nor A+E=[1 1 ; 1 1] is the zero matrix. The product of two matrices that are not the zero matrix can be O, so unlike numbers, you cannot say "one of the two is 0."
y-m-43-05.s.s3.modelNote.2: An answer that gives zero divisors (two non-zero matrices whose product is O) as the reason.

y-m-43-06.title: Can we trust it because one pair worked?
y-m-43-06.topic: Determinants and sums of matrices: |A+B| and |A|+|B|
y-m-43-06.goal: Evaluate a generalization that takes a pair that happened to work as evidence that it holds, make matrices for which the formula breaks and check under what condition it breaks, and write a rebuttal based on that result.
y-m-43-06.material: A matrix is written row by row, and what is before the semicolon (;) is the first row. For example, [1 1 ; 0 1] is the matrix whose first row is 1, 1 and second row is 0, 1. E is the identity matrix [1 0 ; 0 1], and O is the zero matrix with all entries 0. The determinant of a 2×2 matrix M=[a b ; c d] is written |M|=ad-bc. Doyun said, 'The determinant of the sum of two matrices equals the sum of their determinants. That is, |A+B|=|A|+|B|.' As evidence, he tested A=[1 0 ; 0 0] and B=[0 1 ; 1 0], and |A+B|=|[1 1 ; 1 0]|=-1 and |A|+|B|=0+(-1)=-1, which were equal.
y-m-43-06.thinking.0: Evaluate the strength of the evidence
y-m-43-06.thinking.1: Make a counterexample directly and check the condition under which it breaks
y-m-43-06.thinking.2: Write a rebuttal together with its grounds
y-m-43-06.prereq.0: This task's H3 is only a marker of the difficulty and support level of this production assignment, not a sign that the curriculum assigns it to that grade. It assumes you have already learned the definition of a matrix and the sum, product, and identity matrix of 2×2 matrices.
y-m-43-06.prereq.1: Calculating the determinant |M|=ad-bc of a 2×2 matrix (M=[a b ; c d])
y-m-43-06.s.s1.prompt: Choose the most suitable evaluation of Doyun's evidence.
y-m-43-06.s.s1.hint.0: Count how many 0s there are in the entries of the A and B that Doyun tested, and think about how that affects the calculation.
y-m-43-06.s.s1.hint.1: Change A or B to other matrices and compare |A+B| and |A|+|B| directly.
y-m-43-06.s.s1.o.a: Since one pair held, we may assume other pairs hold too
y-m-43-06.s.s1.r.a: This is a judgment that extended one success to all cases. The test of looking for pairs where it does not hold is missing.
y-m-43-06.s.s1.o.b: There is an example where it holds, so the claim is judged false
y-m-43-06.s.s1.r.b: An example where it holds does not make a claim false. What makes it false is an example where it does not hold (a counterexample).
y-m-43-06.s.s1.o.c: The proof is done with one pair, so we only need to check there is no calculation mistake, and no counterexample is needed
y-m-43-06.s.s1.r.c: This is a judgment that took one example as proving 'always'. Even if the calculation is right, the range that pair represents is narrow.
y-m-43-06.s.s1.o.d: One pair is weak evidence, so we should test more to see whether there are pairs that break it
y-m-43-06.s.s1.explain: One example where it holds is weak evidence that a claim is true. This time most of the entries of A were 0, so the two values happened to match. To test a claim, you must look for pairs that break it.
y-m-43-06.s.s2.prompt: When A is the identity matrix E=[1 0 ; 0 1], make three B=[p q ; r s] for which |E+B| and |E|+|B| differ. Make the entries integers, and B for which the values of (p+s) and |B| are both the same are counted as the same example.
y-m-43-06.s.s2.hint.0: Let the entries of B be p, q, r, s and write E+B and its determinant.
y-m-43-06.s.s2.hint.1: Put the two expanded expressions for |E+B| and |E|+|B| side by side and find what part is different.
y-m-43-06.s.s2.var.p: Entry p in the first row, first column of B
y-m-43-06.s.s2.var.q: Entry q in the first row, second column of B
y-m-43-06.s.s2.var.r: Entry r in the second row, first column of B
y-m-43-06.s.s2.var.s: Entry s in the second row, second column of B
y-m-43-06.s.s2.ok.c1: The entries are integers from -5 to 5.
y-m-43-06.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make the entries integers from -5 to 5.
y-m-43-06.s.s2.ok.c2: |E+B| and |E|+|B| are different. Doyun's formula broke.
y-m-43-06.s.s2.fail.c2: |E+B| and |E|+|B| are the same. Write the two values in terms of p, q, r, s and compare.
y-m-43-06.s.s2.explain: |E+B|=(1+p)(1+s)-qr=1+(p+s)+(ps-qr) and |E|+|B|=1+(ps-qr). Their difference is p+s, that is, the sum of the two diagonal entries of B. So if p+s≠0, Doyun's formula breaks, and if p+s=0, it happens to hold for this A (=E). The pair Doyun first tested was also such a coincidence.
y-m-43-06.s.s3.prompt: Write a reply to send to Doyun. Using one example you made above, show that Doyun's formula does not always hold, and write one reason why the one pair Doyun tested could not reveal this.
y-m-43-06.s.s3.hint.0: With one B you made above, write E+B and write its determinant as a number.
y-m-43-06.s.s3.hint.1: Compare the entries of the A and B that Doyun tested with the B you just made and say what difference there is.
y-m-43-06.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you show the values of |E+B| and |E|+|B| in your counterexample as numbers?
y-m-43-06.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you connect why 'it worked once' is not 'it always works' to Doyun's test (most of the entries of A are 0)?
y-m-43-06.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you think about whether it would be even better to mention the condition you found (if the sum of B's diagonal entries is 0, it holds for this A)?
y-m-43-06.s.s3.model.0: It doesn't always hold. If A=E and B=[1 0 ; 0 0], then |E+B|=|[2 0 ; 0 1]|=2 but |E|+|B|=1+0=1. The one pair you tested was a case that happened to work.
y-m-43-06.s.s3.model.1: There is a counterexample. Adding E and [2 0 ; 0 1] gives [3 0 ; 0 2] and its determinant is 6, but 1+2=3, so they differ. One pair working does not mean every pair works, and your example had many 0s among the entries.
y-m-43-06.s.s3.modelNote.1: A model answer that gives the counterexample and reason with other numbers.

y-m-43-07.title: When can we be sure about a repeating pattern?
y-m-43-07.topic: Repeating rules (periods) in powers of a matrix
y-m-43-07.material: A matrix is written row by row, and what is before the semicolon (;) is the first row. For example, [1 1 ; 0 1] is the matrix whose first row is 1, 1 and second row is 0, 1. E is the identity matrix [1 0 ; 0 1], and O is the zero matrix with all entries 0. You will find out how the powers A^n (A multiplied n times) of the matrix A=[0 -1 ; 1 0] change. The calculation results are revealed step by step.
y-m-43-07.thinking.0: Guess a rule from partial information and weigh the strength of the evidence
y-m-43-07.thinking.1: Confirm or revise the judgment with new information
y-m-43-07.thinking.2: Find a large power using the rule and explain it
y-m-43-07.prereq.0: This task's H3 is only a marker of the difficulty and support level of this production assignment, not a sign that the curriculum assigns it to that grade. It assumes you have already learned the definition of a matrix and the sum, product, and identity matrix of 2×2 matrices.
y-m-43-07.prereq.2: A feel for the fact that multiplying by -E only changes the sign
y-m-43-07.prereq.3: Calculating repetition by remainders (the remainder of a division)
y-m-43-07.s.s1.prompt: Each time a result is revealed, choose the most reasonable judgment with the evidence now. If the judgment you made in an earlier step should be revised now, revise it, and if the evidence is still enough, you may keep it.
y-m-43-07.s.s1.hint.0: Compare the matrix newly obtained at each step with the previous matrix and look at what shape appears again.
y-m-43-07.s.s1.hint.1: Check by direct multiplication what happens when you multiply the previous result by A once more.
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.0.ask: How do you think A^3, A^4, … will continue? What is the most reasonable judgment from the calculations so far?
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.0.after: a is a guess that A^3=A·A^2=-A and A^4=(A^2)^2=E from the rules of multiplication, and b is wanting to calculate more to confirm. Both are reasonable. In the next step, check A^3 and A^4.
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.0.o.a: A^2=-E, so the shape will probably repeat, like A^3=-A and A^4=E
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.0.r.a: You guessed the next shape using the fact that multiplying by -E changes the sign.
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.0.o.b: We cannot know from just two, so we should calculate A^3 and A^4 too
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is a careful judgment that saw the evidence as lacking and wanted to calculate more.
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.0.o.c: A^2 is -E, so -E keeps coming out after that
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.0.r.c: A^3=A·A^2, so just because A^2 is -E does not mean A^3 is also -E. Check what happens when you multiply A by -E.
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.0.o.d: The more powers we take, the larger the entries will get
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.0.r.d: The entries that have come out so far are only -1, 0, 1. Look for evidence that they grow.
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.1.info: I checked by calculation that A^3=[0 1 ; -1 0] (= -A) and A^4=[1 0 ; 0 1] (= E).
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.1.after: A^4=E, so A^100=(A^4)^25=E. A, -E, -A, E repeat every four.
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.1.r.a: This may be a judgment that took the remainder of 100 divided by 4 to be 1. Calculate the remainder again.
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.1.r.b: This may be a guess that came from A^2 being -E. Check that A^4 was E and how many times 4 goes into 100.
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.1.r.c: A^4=E, so it is the 25th power of (A^4).
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.1.r.d: This may be a guess that came from A^3 being -A. Check whether the remainder of 100 divided by 4 is 3.
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.2.after: B^3=-E, so B^6=(B^3)^2=E. 100=6×16+4, so B^100=B^4=B·B^3=-B. A repeats every four, and B repeats every six.
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.2.r.a: This may be a judgment that used the period 4 found for A as it is (100 is a multiple of 4). Check whether B^4 is E for B as well.
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.2.r.c: Check at which of B^1, B^4, B^7 the shape starts again.
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.2.r.d: This may be a guess that came from B^3 being -E. Think together about the remainder of 100 divided by 3 and B^6.
y-m-43-07.s.s1.st.2.r.e: B^2 is not the shape that follows B^1, B^2, B^3. Look for the exponent at which E comes out.
y-m-43-07.s.s1.reflect: For A it repeated every four, and for B every six. The rule (period) differs by matrix, and using a number found for one matrix as it is for another matrix can be wrong. Say how your judgment changed before and after the new information in step 3 (B^3=-E), and whether your first judgment for A had enough evidence.
y-m-43-07.s.s2.prompt: For A=[0 -1 ; 1 0], find A^2026 and write how you found it.
y-m-43-07.s.s2.hint.0: Write A^1 to A^4 in order and find at which exponent it first becomes E.
y-m-43-07.s.s2.hint.1: Find the quotient and remainder when 2026 is divided by that exponent, and find in the table the shape that the remainder points to.
y-m-43-07.s.s2.selfAssess.0: Is the method you wrote one that uses the repeating rule, not 'multiply 2026 times'?
y-m-43-07.s.s2.selfAssess.1: Did you find the remainder of 2026 divided by 4 correctly?
y-m-43-07.s.s2.selfAssess.2: Can you also say what A^2027 or A^2028 would be by the same method?
y-m-43-07.s.s2.model.0: A^4=E, so A, -E, -A, E repeat every four. The remainder of 2026 divided by 4 is 2, so A^2026=A^2=-E=[-1 0 ; 0 -1].
y-m-43-07.s.s2.model.1: Multiplying 4 times returns to E, so with 2026=4×506+2, it is the same as multiplying A just 2 times. The result is -E.
y-m-43-07.s.s2.modelNote.1: A model answer written in the form 4×506+2 instead of the remainder.

y-m-43-08.s.s2.var.b: Today's number of customers at 나, b

y-m-43-08.s.s3.prompt: If it starts from 490 at 가 and 510 at 나 today, and these movement rates stay the same, what will happen to the number of customers at 가 from now on? (Tomorrow 가 is 0.7×490+100=443.)
y-m-43-08.s.s3.hint.0: From today's value, calculate the number of customers at 가 for tomorrow, the day after, and the day after that, in order, and write them in a table.

y-m-43-08.s.s3.o.b: It stays near the same 443 every day

y-m-43-09.title: If there are two equations, is there only one solution?
y-m-43-09.topic: Solutions of a system of linear equations and the coefficient matrix
y-m-43-09.goal: Without concluding that there is one solution just because the number of unknowns and equations are the same, tell apart cases where there are no solutions or many depending on the coefficients and the value on the right, and build equations whose solution is fixed to one and which satisfy a condition.
y-m-43-09.material: A matrix is written row by row, and what is before the semicolon (;) is the first row. For example, [1 1 ; 0 1] is the matrix whose first row is 1, 1 and second row is 0, 1. E is the identity matrix [1 0 ; 0 1], and O is the zero matrix with all entries 0. The system of linear equations x+2y=4, 2x+ny=k is written with matrices as [1 2 ; 2 n]·[x ; y]=[4 ; k]. The first equation stays as it is, and the coefficient n of y in the second equation and the value k on the right are revealed step by step. x and y are real numbers. Hajun thinks, 'There are 2 unknowns and 2 equations, so there will be one solution.'
y-m-43-09.thinking.0: Tell apart what can and cannot be said at a stage where information is insufficient
y-m-43-09.thinking.1: Confirm or revise judgments with new information
y-m-43-09.thinking.2: Design equations that satisfy a condition directly
y-m-43-09.prereq.0: This task's H3 is only a marker of the difficulty and support level of this production assignment, not a sign that the curriculum assigns it to that grade. It assumes you have already learned the definition of a matrix and the sum, product, and identity matrix of 2×2 matrices.
y-m-43-09.prereq.1: Solving a system of linear equations (middle school grade 2 level)
y-m-43-09.prereq.2: The experience of having seen once the meaning of the determinant ad-bc of a 2×2 matrix
y-m-43-09.s.s1.prompt: Each time information is revealed, choose the most reasonable judgment with the evidence now. If the judgment must be revised, revise it, and if the evidence is still enough, you may keep it.
y-m-43-09.s.s1.hint.0: Put the left sides of the two equations (the coefficients of x and y) side by side and compare how many times one equation is the other.
y-m-43-09.s.s1.hint.1: Once the value on the right is decided, check whether the same multiple relation holds on the right too.
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.0.info: The coefficient of y in the second equation is n=4. The value k on the right is not yet known: x+2y=4, 2x+4y=k.
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.0.ask: Now that you do not know k, what can be said about the solutions of this system of equations?
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.0.after: Looking only at the left coefficients, the left side of the second equation is 2 times the left side of the first (2x+4y=2(x+2y)). So whatever k is, there is no case where the solution is fixed to one, and it splits depending on k. The value on the right is revealed in the next step.
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.0.o.a: Whatever k is, there is exactly one solution
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.0.r.a: This is the generalization that 2 unknowns with 2 equations means one solution. Compare the left sides of the two equations and check how many times one equation is the other.
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.0.o.b: Depending on k there are no solutions or infinitely many, and there is no k with only one
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.0.r.b: This is a judgment that, based on the left coefficients being proportional, the solution is not fixed to one regardless of k.
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.0.o.c: Depending on k there is one solution or none
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.0.r.c: It is good that you thought of the case with no solution, but check whether there are cases with one solution when the left sides are proportional.
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.0.o.d: We do not know k, so we can say nothing about the solutions and need to know more
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.0.r.d: Even without knowing the value on the right, work out whether there is anything that can be said from the left coefficients alone.
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.1.ask: What happens to the solutions of this system of equations?
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.1.after: The second equation became exactly the same as 2 times the first (2x+4y=8 is x+2y=4 with both sides multiplied by 2). So the two equations are actually the same equation, and every (x, y) satisfying x+2y=4 is a solution.
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.1.o.a: There is no solution. The two equations contradict each other
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.1.r.a: Compare the second equation 2x+4y=8 with 2 times the first. Check whether a contradiction arises.
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.1.r.b: It is true that (0, 2) is a solution, but you did not check whether there are other solutions. Put in (4, 0).
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.1.o.c: The solutions are only the two, (4, 0) and (0, 2)
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.1.r.c: It is true that the two points are solutions, but you did not check whether points between them or other points are solutions. Put in (2, 1).
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.1.o.d: There are infinitely many solutions. (2, 1) is also a solution
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.2.info: This value was measured with a scale and read as k=9: x+2y=4, 2x+4y=9. (It is not certain that k is exactly 9.)
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.2.ask: What is a reasonable judgment about this system of equations?
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.2.after: It should be 2(x+2y)=8, but the second equation says 9, which is a contradiction. If k=9 is exact, there is no solution. Because it is a measured value and uncertain, option d, that k should be checked again, is also reasonable.
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.2.o.a: If k=9 is exact, there is no solution
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.2.r.b: Putting (2, 1) into the second equation gives 5, which does not match 9. Think again about whether there is one solution when the left sides are proportional.
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.2.r.c: This may be using the judgment from k=8 as it is. Check how the second equation differs from 2 times the first when k changes to 9.
y-m-43-09.s.s1.st.2.o.d: There is no solution. But first we should check whether k is exactly 9
y-m-43-09.s.s1.reflect: The moment n=4 made the left coefficients proportional, the case where the solution is fixed to one disappeared whatever k is, and it split into infinitely many if k=8 and none otherwise. You must not conclude there is one solution just because the number of equations and the number of unknowns are the same. Say at which step you confirmed your judgment and at which step you changed it with new information.
y-m-43-09.s.s2.prompt: Change the second equation to 2x+ny=k and make three (n, k) with different n for which the solution is fixed to one and, at that solution, x and y are both positive and y is less than 2. (The first equation stays x+2y=4.)
y-m-43-09.s.s2.hint.0: In the second equation 2x+ny=k, compare how the shape seen earlier differs when n is 4 and when n is not 4.
y-m-43-09.s.s2.hint.1: Decide one n, express x in terms of y from the first equation, put it into the second equation, and write y as an expression in k.
y-m-43-09.s.s2.var.n: The coefficient n of y in the second equation
y-m-43-09.s.s2.var.k: The value k on the right of the second equation
y-m-43-09.s.s2.ok.c1: n is not 4, so the left sides of the two equations are not proportional.
y-m-43-09.s.s2.fail.c1: If n is 4, the left sides are proportional and the solution is not fixed to one.
y-m-43-09.s.s2.ok.c2: In the solution, y is greater than 0.
y-m-43-09.s.s2.fail.c2: In the solution, y is 0 or less. Express x in terms of y from the first equation, put it into the second equation, and write y in terms of n and k.
y-m-43-09.s.s2.ok.c3: In the solution, y is less than 2. So x=4-2y is also positive.
y-m-43-09.s.s2.fail.c3: In the solution, y is 2 or more. x=4-2y must be positive.
y-m-43-09.s.s2.explain: If n is not 4, one solution is fixed by y=(k-8)/(n-4), x=4-2y. For example, with n=5 and k=9, y=1 and x=2, and with n=6 and k=9, y=1/2 and x=3. y must be greater than 0 and less than 2 for x to be positive too.

y-m-43-10.title: Making a key to undo integer notes
y-m-43-10.topic: Designing a key matrix that has an inverse matrix with integer entries
y-m-43-10.goal: Judge whether a key matrix can be used, design directly a key that can be undone with integer calculation alone, and explain that condition with the inverse matrix formula.
y-m-43-10.material: A matrix is written row by row, and what is before the semicolon (;) is the first row. For example, [1 1 ; 0 1] is the matrix whose first row is 1, 1 and second row is 0, 1. E is the identity matrix [1 0 ; 0 1], and O is the zero matrix with all entries 0. Two integers (x, y) are treated as the column vector [x ; y], and the key matrix K=[a b ; c d] multiplied from the left, [ax+by ; cx+dy], is sent as a note. The receiving side is a device that can calculate only integers, so it multiplies the inverse matrix of K onto the note to recover the original (x, y), but it cannot be used if the entries of the inverse matrix have fractions. Inverse matrix formula: if ad-bc≠0, then K^(-1) = (1/(ad-bc)) · [d -b ; -c a].
y-m-43-10.thinking.0: Sort out keys that cannot be used by counterexamples
y-m-43-10.thinking.1: Design several keys that satisfy the constraints
y-m-43-10.thinking.2: Explain with the formula why the condition is needed
y-m-43-10.prereq.0: This task's H3 is only a marker of the difficulty and support level of this production assignment, not a sign that the curriculum assigns it to that grade. It assumes you have already learned the definition of a matrix and the sum, product, and identity matrix of 2×2 matrices.
y-m-43-10.prereq.1: Products of 2×2 matrices and the calculation of multiplying a column vector by a matrix
y-m-43-10.prereq.2: The experience of having seen once the inverse matrix formula of a 2×2 matrix (the formula is written in the text)
y-m-43-10.s.s1.prompt: Cheolsu says he will use K=[2 1 ; 4 2] as the key. Choose the most suitable judgment about this key.
y-m-43-10.s.s1.hint.0: Multiply K onto two different integer pairs (1, 1) and (0, 3) and compare the results.
y-m-43-10.s.s1.hint.1: Find the value of ad-bc of K and check whether it can be put into the inverse matrix formula.
y-m-43-10.s.s1.o.a: It cannot be used. There are cases where different integer pairs become the same note
y-m-43-10.s.s1.o.b: It can be used. All entries are integers, so integer pairs come back as integers
y-m-43-10.s.s1.r.b: Having integer entries and being able to undo are separate. Choose two different pairs, multiply K onto them, and compare the results.
y-m-43-10.s.s1.o.c: It can be used. No entry is 0, so the mixing is sufficient
y-m-43-10.s.s1.r.c: How much it mixes does not decide whether it can be undone. Check the relation between the first row and the second row.
y-m-43-10.s.s1.o.d: Cannot tell. We can only know by putting it in the inverse matrix formula, and we cannot check whether fractions will come out
y-m-43-10.s.s1.r.d: You can know right away by calculating the denominator ad-bc of the formula. Before fractions come out, first check whether it can be put into the formula at all.
y-m-43-10.s.s1.explain: For K=[2 1 ; 4 2], ad-bc=2×2-1×4=0, so there is no inverse matrix. In fact, multiplying (1, 1) and (0, 3) by K gives (3, 6) for both, so the receiving side cannot decide which one it was.
y-m-43-10.s.s2.prompt: Make three different keys K=[a b ; c d] that the receiving side can undo with integers alone. Conditions: a, b, c, d are integers from -9 to 9 and all non-zero, and K has an inverse matrix whose entries are all integers.
y-m-43-10.s.s2.hint.0: Think about what value the denominator ad-bc must have for fractions not to arise in the inverse matrix formula.
y-m-43-10.s.s2.hint.1: Decide a, b, c first and find d so that ad-bc becomes the value you want.
y-m-43-10.s.s2.var.a: Entry a in the first row, first column
y-m-43-10.s.s2.var.b: Entry b in the first row, second column
y-m-43-10.s.s2.var.c: Entry c in the second row, first column
y-m-43-10.s.s2.var.d: Entry d in the second row, second column
y-m-43-10.s.s2.ok.c1: The entries are integers from -9 to 9.
y-m-43-10.s.s2.fail.c1: Please make the entries integers from -9 to 9.
y-m-43-10.s.s2.fail.c2: There is an entry that is 0. Please make them all non-zero.
y-m-43-10.s.s2.ok.c3: There is an inverse matrix and its entries are all integers.
y-m-43-10.s.s2.fail.c3: There is no inverse matrix, or fractions arise in the inverse matrix. Check the value of the denominator ad-bc of the inverse matrix formula.
y-m-43-10.s.s3.prompt: Write what value ad-bc must have for all the entries of the inverse matrix to be integers, and explain the reason in one or two sentences using the inverse matrix formula.
y-m-43-10.s.s3.hint.0: Pick a key with ad-bc equal to 2, put it into the inverse matrix formula, and write what the entries become.
y-m-43-10.s.s3.hint.1: Write what number the front part of the formula, 1/(ad-bc), is when ad-bc is 1, -1, 2, 3.
y-m-43-10.s.s3.selfAssess.0: Did you write the values of ad-bc (two of them) without missing any?
y-m-43-10.s.s3.selfAssess.1: Did you connect 'why it must be that value' to the denominator of the formula K^(-1)=(1/(ad-bc))·[d -b ; -c a]?
y-m-43-10.s.s3.selfAssess.2: Did you check with the formula why a key with ad-bc equal to 2 (for example [1 1 ; -1 1]) cannot be undone with integers alone?
y-m-43-10.s.s3.model.0: ad-bc must be 1 or -1. The inverse matrix is d, -b, -c, a divided by ad-bc, so if ad-bc is 2 or 3 fractions arise, and if it is 1 or -1 the entries stay integers after dividing.
y-m-43-10.s.s3.model.1: The determinant must be ±1. The entries of the inverse matrix are fractions like d/(ad-bc), and only if the denominator is ±1 do all the entries remain integers.
y-m-43-10.s.s3.modelNote.1: A model answer written with the ±1 symbol and the denominator.
y-m-43-10.s.s2.explain: For example, K=[2 1 ; 1 1] has ad-bc=1 and K^(-1)=[1 -1 ; -1 2], and K=[1 2 ; 1 1] has ad-bc=-1 and K^(-1)=[-1 2 ; 1 -1]. All entries are integers, so you can undo it using only integers. For all entries of the inverse matrix to be integers, ad-bc must divide all of a, b, c, d, and then (ad-bc)² divides ad-bc, so ad-bc must be 1 or -1.
y-m-43-10.s.s3.model.2: ad−bc is ±1. The entries of the inverse matrix are numbers obtained by dividing d or -b by ad−bc, so if the size of ad-bc is greater than 1, they will not be integers.
